title: Quick sort
summary: Pick a pivot, partition, repeat. Fast on average, with a catch.

cards.title: Pick a pivot
cards.body:
Choose one value, the **pivot**. Move everything smaller to its left and everything bigger to its right. Now the pivot is in its **final position** forever.

Then do the same on the left part and the right part. That's quicksort.
Gold = the pivot. `store` marks where the next small value will go.

cards.title: The code (Lomuto partition)
cards.body: `partition` uses the last element as the pivot. `store` grows the "smaller than pivot" zone from the left. At the end, the pivot swaps into `store`, its final spot.

cards.title: The catch
cards.body:
If the pivot splits the range roughly in half, quicksort is **O(n log n)** and very fast in practice (no extra buffer, cache friendly).

But with "last element" as pivot, an **already sorted** list is the worst input: every partition peels off just one value. That's n levels of n work: **O(n²)**.

Real libraries defend against this: `std::sort` uses **introsort**, which switches to heap sort if the recursion gets too deep.

cards.question: Using the last element as pivot, which input makes this quicksort slowest?
cards.explain: On sorted input the pivot is always the biggest value, so each partition only removes one element. That gives O(n²).
